verdicts.summary: The paper introduces aiprov, a PROV-O extension for recording AI-in-the-loop work (three agent classes, four activity classes, claims/sources/prompts/transcripts as entities, full inference telemetry), governed by two invariants — no parentless claim, and a seven-rung verification ladder whose top two rungs only humans may grant — enforced by a seven-check SPARQL validator that doubles as a CI gate. The method is packaged as an executable Agent Skill that an AI agent operates on itself (ORCID-first setup, two-commit binding discipline, CI-built PDF and disclosure, an issue-based path for authenticated human rung grants), and the paper is its own case study: its production is recorded in a 3,100-triple graph including incidents, telemetry (~2.5M output tokens, ~USD 1,577 computed cost, ~10% measured bookkeeping overhead), and a deliberately bounded novelty claim scoped to a logged registry-sweep search horizon. The claimed contribution is not any single component but the combination of human-only verification rungs, executable-skill packaging, and self-application, positioned against PROV-AGENT as nearest neighbor.
strengths: The repository genuinely is the evidence: I verified that the seven validator checks described in §4 correspond one-to-one to the SPARQL queries in provlog.py (four hard failures, three warnings, exit-code contract as stated), that CI gates on validation, that the 8 claims, 67 sources, 34 human rung grants, and incident records exist in provenance.ttl, and that the CLI figure's refusal behaviors are implemented. Very few papers in this space survive that level of artifact inspection.

The human-only-rungs idea is a real and, to my knowledge, novel design element: no prior provenance vocabulary machine-encodes 'this verification state may not be granted by an AI agent', separates reference-exists (machine-checkable) from content-supports (machine judgement) from human-checked (human-only), logs every promotion with its grantor, and makes refusal ('checked and not convinced') first-class via aiprov:refusedRung.

The bounded-novelty mechanism — recording the search horizon (registries, query terms, date) as a logged activity so 'no prior work found' becomes a falsifiable, re-runnable claim instead of an unfalsifiable assertion — is an elegant epistemic contribution independent of the rest of the system.

Unusually candid reporting throughout: mishaps, blocked access, and mid-experiment method redesigns are recorded and discussed rather than smoothed over; computed telemetry is explicitly distinguished from provider-reported; cost and the environmental question are disclosed rather than hidden; the scope disclaimer ('a demonstration, not a study; one operator, one domain, one session') is stated before any number; known limits (self-confirmation bias, single-witness telemetry) are named in the paper itself.

The two-commit binding discipline (artefact commit, then graph commit naming it) is a simple, well-argued tamper-evidence design with an honest threat model ('honest work is cheap, dishonest work is loud'), and the dual-witness discussion of provider-signed inference records is careful about what signing does and does not prove.

Several practices are immediately adoptable and clearly explained: registry-fetched BibTeX via DOI content negotiation, verified-before-cited, disclosure statements derived from the graph at build time, and the rung-4 access gate that hands the human the evidence before requesting judgement.

The paper is well written, correctly scoped in its explicit novelty claim (a combination claim, not component claims), and honest that PROV-AGENT already provides per-activity AI provenance on the same substrate.
weaknesses: Related work has substantive gaps that weaken the novelty positioning: nanopublications (Groth/Mons line, 2010) and micropublications (Clark et al., 2014) made claims first-class citizens with attached provenance long before '§3: aiprov's answer makes claims first-class'; C2PA/Content Credentials is the industry standard for signed, machine-readable provenance of AI-generated content and is directly relevant to both the EU-AI-Act marking argument and the dual-witness discussion; in-toto/SLSA supply-chain attestations already bind artefacts to process steps with signed records; and Manubot has provided CI-built manuscripts with DOI-content-negotiation citation metadata since ~2019, i.e., two of §7's 'practices that emerged' are prior art. None of these are cited.

Verified ontology defect: aiprov:verificationState is declared rdfs:domain aiprov:Claim in assets/aiprov-schema.ttl, yet all 67 aiprov:Source instances in provenance.ttl carry it and none has prov:wasGeneratedBy — under RDFS entailment every source is a parentless Claim, so the graph violates Invariant I under the schema's own semantics; the validator passes only because it queries without inference. For a paper whose lineage argument is 'semantics must be formal and machine-readable', this matters.

Invariant II's hard enforcement is string matching, not semantics: AI-granted human rungs are detected by REGEX over English rdfs:label text ('-> human-confirmed'); promotions have no structured representation (no aiprov:grantedRung mirroring aiprov:refusedRung), so a differently-worded promotion label silently evades the hard check, and a rung written directly into the graph draws only a warning. SHACL, the standard RDF conformance mechanism, is neither used nor discussed.

The ladder conflates evidential strength with access/process state: source-vendored (position 4, 'of no evidential value by itself' per the paper's own definition) outranks ai-confirmed (3), and needs-research (a failed check) outranks unverified, so the schema's 'higher position = stronger check' is false for two of seven rungs; because verificationState is single-valued and promotions strictly climb, promoting a content-checked source to vendored erases the visible content-check state (recoverable only from free-text audit labels). Splitting access state from verification state would resolve this.

Metric hygiene: build_metrics.py counts source-vendored as 'checked', so Table 2's 'thereof at ai-confirmed or above: 65' includes 24 sources at a rung the paper defines as asserting nothing about content — and many of those are the paper's own section files (02-background-tex, README-md, SKILL-md, ...) registered as Sources, mixing repository-internal artefacts into what reads as a bibliography-verification statistic.

Claim coverage is discretionary and sparse: 8 Claim nodes for ~8,800 words of prose, all about the tooling plus the novelty claim; none of the paper's substantive scholarly assertions (the dilution argument, the discussion positions) are claims in the graph. 'No parentless claim' governs only claims someone chose to register; the paper states no policy for what must become a Claim, so the invariant is trivially satisfiable by registering little, and the abstract's 'every activity, claim, and source in its production is recorded' oversells what the record contains.

The self-application cannot fail as an evaluation: the criterion is the method's own validator, the evaluator is the authoring agent, and every claim sits at that agent's own ai-confirmed ceiling; there is no second operator, no second domain, no baseline comparison against conventional record-keeping, and completeness of the record is unverifiable in principle from within (an unrecorded activity leaves no trace). The paper acknowledges nearly all of this, which is to its credit, but acknowledgement does not substitute for evaluation; as it stands the meta-experiment demonstrates feasibility and honesty, not effectiveness.

The in-session human-grant path is unauthenticated: rungs 5–6 granted 'in the session' are transcribed by the AI from a chat message ('confirm aas idta') with the human agent ID passed as a CLI flag; only the GitHub-issue path verifies identity against doc/operators.json. The human-only invariant is thus enforced against honest tooling use, not against the graph's writer — a sharper statement of this asymmetry belongs in §7.

The executed bounded-novelty sweep is too thin to carry the claim it parents: activity s47 records two query strings over Crossref with OpenAlex rate-limited, and it demonstrably missed near neighbors (nanopublications, Manubot, C2PA) that keyword sweeps over one registry cannot reach. The mechanism is sound; this instance shows a narrow horizon can render the bounded claim near-vacuous, and the sweep should be widened and re-recorded before publication.

The worked example (§5, ultrasonic welding) is a design sketch written in the present tense — 'CI reruns the analysis, so a figure that cannot be regenerated from the recorded inputs fails the build' is implemented nowhere in the repository (CI validates the graph and compiles LaTeX) — and should be marked as prospective.
The w3id.org/aiprov vocabulary namespace returns 404 at review time: the central identifier of a FAIR-infrastructure paper does not itself resolve (FAIR F1/A1).

Sections 3 and 7 are discursive (dilution essay, copyright, environmental cost, 'nostalgia for the paper'); engaging, but some of that space is owed to a proper related-work treatment of the missed lines above. The executable-skill packaging itself is competent engineering rather than a research result; the paper is honest that the contribution is the combination, but the venue should weigh it as such.
questions: The vocabulary namespace https://w3id.org/aiprov/ns returns 404 at review time. Is registration pending, and will the schema be served with content negotiation before camera-ready?

aiprov:verificationState has rdfs:domain aiprov:Claim but is asserted on all 67 Sources, none of which has prov:wasGeneratedBy — under RDFS entailment the graph violates your own Invariant I. Will you widen the domain and re-validate with entailment enabled?

Why are promotions detected by regex over rdfs:label rather than a structured property (e.g., aiprov:grantedRung, mirroring aiprov:refusedRung)? A differently-worded label would evade the hard check for Invariant II — have you considered SHACL shapes for the conformance contract?

What is the intended policy for which textual assertions must become aiprov:Claim nodes? The graph holds 8 claims for ~8,800 words, all about the tooling; what prevents an adopter from satisfying 'no parentless claim' by registering almost nothing?

How do you position aiprov against nanopublications and micropublications (claims-as-first-class with provenance), C2PA content credentials (signed AI-content provenance), in-toto/SLSA attestations (signed artefact-to-process binding), and Manubot (CI-built manuscripts with DOI-content-negotiation citations)?

Table 2 reports 65 of 67 sources 'at ai-confirmed or above', but 24 of these sit at source-vendored — a rung you define as having no evidential value — and many are the paper's own section files registered as Sources. Will you separate literature sources from repository-internal artefacts and report vendored-only separately?

Since verificationState is single-valued and promotions strictly climb, promoting an ai-confirmed source to source-vendored erases the visible content-check state. Would splitting access state (vendored/link-only) from verification state resolve both this and the ladder-ordering incoherence (needs-research above unverified)?

Is the in-session human-grant path authenticated in any way, or is the GitHub-issue path the only one where the granting human's identity is verified rather than transcribed by the AI from a chat message?
Is the §5 welding example's 'CI reruns the analysis' implemented anywhere, or is the worked example prospective? Please mark it accordingly.

The s47 novelty sweep is two query strings over Crossref (OpenAlex rate-limited). Given that it missed nanopublications, Manubot, and C2PA, will you re-run a wider sweep (Semantic Scholar/DBLP/arXiv full-text, additional query formulations) and re-record the horizon before publication?

verdicts.summary: The paper introduces "aiprov", a PROV-O extension for recording who (human, AI, or tool) did what in AI-in-the-loop research work, with two invariants (no parentless claim; a seven-rung verification ladder whose top two rungs only humans may grant), packages the method as an executable Agent Skill that an AI agent operates on itself (ORCID-first setup, two-commit binding discipline, CI conformance gating, auto-generated EU-AI-Act disclosure), and evaluates it via a meta-experiment: the paper's own production is the case study, and its committed provenance graph, transcript, incidents, and cost record (229 activities, 67 ladder-backed sources, ~2.5M output tokens, computed cost ~USD 1,577) are the evaluation object. The paper explicitly scopes itself as a demonstration (one operator, one domain, one session), discusses self-report honesty, the single-witness problem, self-confirmation bias, and cost, and asks providers for signed inference records as the missing second witness.
strengths: The central claim — the repo IS the evidence — largely survives adversarial spot-checking. I ran the validator on the actual graph (7 checks as described in §4: 4 hard, 3 warnings; exits 0), reproduced Figure 5's human-only-rung refusal verbatim on a sandbox copy of the graph, and confirmed graph counts against provenance.ttl: 8 claims all ai-confirmed, 67 sources, 5 marked selfCitation, 34 human rungs (32 human-confirmed + 2 human-read), pass counts 66/151/2/10, and agent associations 194 AI / 36 human / 2 CI — all matching Table II/III within the disclosed regeneration lag.

Session-derived numbers reproduce. From the session record I independently recomputed token totals (matching metrics.json to within the record's continued growth), the cost arithmetic ($1,577.29 exactly from the stated $10/$50/$1/$20 price basis, with cache_write_5m=0 verified in code so the all-1h-TTL claim holds), active hours (12.1–12.2 h) and 89 h span, and — importantly — the paper's 'no request mixed bookkeeping with substantive work' claim: my recount found 0 mixed requests among 2,460, confirming a claim the published script does not itself compute.

Unusually rigorous honesty engineering: omit-don't-estimate applied even to counterfactuals (no solo-baseline estimate); cost explicitly labeled computed-not-provider-reported with the price basis printed in the table footnote and in metrics.json _methodology; the Opus/Sonnet rows correctly framed as price-basis comparisons, not run predictions; incidents (section-overwrite mishap with named restoring commit 75d21bd, which exists in history; malformed registry BibTeX; publisher 403s; two operator-contested ladder redesigns; three repaired citation overreaches) recorded as ordinary activities, with repair labels even recording rejected audit findings.

Single-source-of-numbers discipline is real: every number in the paper is a macro generated by scripts/build_metrics.py, with methodology strings shipped in doc/metrics.json; no hand-typed quantities found.

Scoping discipline is respected: 'this is a demonstration, not a study; one operator, one domain, one session' is stated in §6 before any number; the conclusion explicitly names self-confirmation bias (AI verified sources for sentences it wrote) and the need for a second operator/second domain as owed trials; §7 honestly analyzes why even provider-signed records would not be tamper-proof (key custody, API-seam coverage, judgement vs. attestation).

The originality claim is exemplary in form: bounded to a recorded search horizon, with the novelty sweep logged in the graph including query terms and the nearest neighbor (PROV-AGENT) named and cited rather than omitted.

The verification ladder's semantics are carefully thought through (vendoring explicitly stripped of evidential value and repositioned as an access gate; human-read defined as read-AND-confirm; refusals logged as first-class), and content-check promotion notes in the graph genuinely carry supporting quotations and checked depth as §6 claims (spot-checked several).
weaknesses: The primary record behind most quantitative results is not in the repository. Table II's token/cost rows, the entire overhead analysis (Fig. 7), and the leverage metrics derive from the agent session .jsonl (per-request usage blocks, full tool-call inputs), which lives outside the repo and is not a release asset; the committed transcript truncates tool inputs at 400 chars / outputs at 700 chars and omits usage entirely. §6's claim that 'a sceptic can recompute or contest any of them' therefore outruns the published evidence — I could recompute only because the session record happened to be present in this environment; an external auditor cloning the repo cannot. §6's closing paragraph concedes only that the honesty of telemetry is uncheckable; the stronger fact — that mechanical recomputation is impossible from the published record — goes unstated.

A concrete metrics bug: Table II's '1 session, 3,634 turns' is inflated ~14%. build_metrics.py counts every '\n## ' occurrence in the transcript markdown, which counts markdown headings inside message bodies (pasted skill docs, tool-result content) as turns; actual turn headers (Human/Assistant/Tool result/Hook) number ~3,189. Ironic for a paper about measurement discipline, and exactly the kind of error the single-source pipeline was meant to preclude.

Per-activity inference telemetry — a headline feature of the aiprov schema ('full inference telemetry', §1) — is populated for only 2 of 232 activities: the two aggregate backfill records covering ~47% of session cost ($736.95 in the graph vs. $1,577 in Table II). The dashboard caption discloses that the tiles 'differ' from the table, but not the magnitude: essentially no activity in the demonstration carries its own token counts, and roughly half the session's usage is attributed to no activity at all. The harness limitation is honestly narrated, but the gap between schema pitch and demonstrated record deserves explicit quantification.

Human-only rung enforcement is weaker than §4/§5's rhetoric suggests. The CLI refuses '--agent <AI>', but the AI executes promotions naming the human as agent: 13 of the 34 human rungs were transcribed in-session from chat messages ('confirm my selfcitations'), where the graph entry asserting a human granted the rung was written by the AI, checkable only against the committed transcript; only the 21 issue-path grants carry independent (GitHub-authenticated) evidence of the human's act. The 'validator hard failure' framing invites over-trust; the authenticated-vs-transcribed split is not reported in the paper.

Under-disclosed weakness in the human rungs actually granted: the validator warns that 29 of the 34 human-verified sources are link-only (mutable audit targets) — the method's own flag for a weaker grant. The paper mentions this warning class only for the 5 self-citations and never reports the 29/34 prevalence. Relatedly, all 8 recorded claims remain at ai-confirmed: the human rungs were exercised solely on sources, never on the paper's own claims, and the operator's assertion of having 'checked all sources and claims' is relayed as an unrecorded report — the one load-bearing statement in §6 with no graph backing.

Snapshot staleness is inherent and unexamined: at review time metrics.json (11:20:25) already lagged provenance.ttl (229 vs. 232 activities, 3,100 vs. 3,162 triples) and git (212 vs. 215 commits), because regenerating metrics itself extends the record. 'Regenerated before submission' cannot converge to a fixpoint; the paper should say which coherent snapshot (e.g., a tagged release) the published numbers describe.

The overhead claim 'upper and lower bounds coincide' is slightly overstated: it rests on zero mixed requests (which I confirmed), but 1,106 of 2,460 requests carry no tool calls and are all classified as substantive; text-only turns inside bookkeeping rounds would be missed, so the ~10% figure is better described as a lower bound under a stated assumption.

Portability is asserted as fact but never demonstrated: 'the skill loads in any Agent Skills client' (Availability) and 'the same bundle loads beyond the environment that produced this paper' (§7) have no supporting record; only three client-specific shims are named. The conclusion concedes second-operator trials are owed, which contradicts the availability note's confidence.

Minor: the prose-word methodology ('LaTeX commands stripped') also deletes command arguments, dropping ~290 content words inside \emph/\texttt/\textbf (true count ~9,080 vs. reported ~8,800); harmless at the stated rounding but sloppy for a paper that invites recomputation. §3 is essayistic relative to the venue norm, and §7's closing self-assessment ('Here, the chance was taken.') grades the authors' own experiment with their own rubric — tonal overreach in an otherwise well-scoped paper.
questions: Will you publish the session record (or a redacted derivative retaining per-request usage blocks, timestamps, and full tool-call inputs) as a release asset so that Table II, the overhead classification, and the leverage figures are actually recomputable by a third party? If not, will you soften §6's 'a sceptic can recompute or contest any of them' accordingly?

Please fix the transcript-turn metric: '\n## ' counting includes markdown headings inside message bodies (~3,634 vs. ~3,189 true turn headers). Will the corrected number propagate through metrics.tex before submission?

How many of the 34 human rungs were granted via the authenticated issue path vs. transcribed in-session by the AI on the operator's chat instruction? Will you report this split, and the 29/34 link-only-audit-target prevalence, in §6?

Why do all 8 claims remain at ai-confirmed when the operator reports having checked them? Granting even one human rung on a claim (not just on sources) would exercise the ladder on the object the method centers on. Is this planned before submission?

Has the skill bundle actually been loaded in a second Agent Skills client, by anyone? If not, please downgrade the availability note's 'loads in any Agent Skills client' to a spec-conformance statement.

Which coherent snapshot (commit/tag) do the published numbers describe, given that regenerating metrics necessarily extends the record it measures? Do you plan to pin the paper's numbers to a tagged release whose assets include graph + metrics + PDF from the same commit?

Only 2 of 232 activities carry token telemetry (the two backfill aggregates, covering roughly half the session's computed cost). Can the exporter attribute usage to activities via request timestamps, or should §1's 'full inference telemetry' be qualified for this demonstration?

verdicts.summary: The paper introduces F(AI)²R — "FAIR research with AI in the loop, twice" — and its concrete contribution "aiprov", a PROV-O extension for recording who (human, AI agent, or deterministic tool) did what in AI-assisted research: activities with full inference telemetry, first-class claims under a "no parentless claim" invariant, and a seven-rung verification ladder whose top two rungs only humans may grant. The method is packaged as an executable "skill" an AI agent operates itself (ORCID-first setup, conformance-gated CI, live preview as an oversight surface), and the paper's central evidentiary move is self-application: the paper's own production is the case study, with its provenance graph, transcripts, incidents (including an agent overwriting committed sections), token/cost accounting, and division-of-labour statistics reported from the public repository, which the authors present as the actual evidence. A long discussion covers self-report honesty and a proposed "dual witness" (provider-signed inference logs), cost/energy accounting, regulatory fit (EU AI Act, OECD, EASA), copyright of largely AI-generated artefacts, self-citation transparency, and whether the paper form is the right artefact to instrument at all.
strengths: Structure is effective and well signposted: motivation (dilution) -> model (method) -> operationalization (skill) -> evaluation (meta-experiment) -> limits; the intro's final paragraph maps contributions to sections, and the meta-experiment opens with an honest scope statement ('this is a demonstration, not a study; one operator, one domain, one session') before any number is given.

Figure 3 (CLI success/failure transcript) is excellent: legible at print size, shows both invariants and the rung-4 access gate actually refusing and then permitting operations, and its caption states capture conditions ('output verbatim; long lines re-wrapped and exit codes annotated'). Table I is similarly self-contained: rung, semantics, and permitted grantor in one place.

Caption discipline is unusually high: screenshots are dated, Figure 6's caption pre-empts the tile-vs-table discrepancy, Figure 7 declares node contents 'abridged from real triples', and Table II's caption states exactly how tokens were obtained and that cost is computed, not provider-reported.

Numbers are single-sourced (metrics.tex generated by scripts/build_metrics.py) and cross-check across the paper: 229 activities, 8 claims, 67 sources, 3100 triples agree between Table II, the Fig. 5 preview badges, and the Fig. 6 dashboard header; I verified this against the repository, which does contain the claimed provenance.ttl, tooling, and transcripts.

The incidents-as-first-class-records subsection is concrete and readable (four typed incidents, each mapped to ordinary vocabulary, one rendered as a real graph excerpt in Fig. 7); reporting the agent's own overwrite mishap materially strengthens the paper's credibility and its 'honesty is the cheap path' argument.

The title/abstract promise is kept: 'who did what' is answered by Table III and the activity ledger, 'who checked' by the ladder and rung-grant records, and 'What the auditor can and cannot verify' honestly bounds the word 'verifiable'.

The prose, while dense, is often memorably precise ('success is quiet and failure is loud'; 'honest work is cheap, dishonest work is loud'; 'omit, don't estimate'), which helps a first-time reader retain the design rules.
weaknesses: The Discussion sprawls: roughly 2.5 of 12 pages across ~13 bold run-in topics (dual witness, cost, skill drift, emergent practices, self-citation, regulation, generality, industry, originality, copyright, nostalgia-for-the-paper, force multiplier). Several are essayistic rather than analytical and partially repeat earlier material; the repository's own outline.md budgeted 0.75 pages for this section. A first-time reader loses the thread of what the limitations actually are.

Claim granularity is never defined. Section III says 'aiprov's answer makes claims first-class. Each assertion carries...', yet the meta-experiment records only 8 claims for a 12-page paper. No criterion is given for which assertions become aiprov:Claim nodes, so the reader cannot tell what 'no parentless claim' guarantees in practice or how trivially it can be satisfied by recording few claims.

Text-figure mismatch in Section VI: 'the remaining sources are deliberately kept at their machine rungs so the demonstration shows every rung in use' sits next to Fig. 6 (bottom), whose distribution shows needs-research = 0 and reference-resolved = 0. If 'in use' means rungs transited historically, the text must say so; as printed, the figure contradicts the sentence.

Fig. 5 (the environment screenshot, the paper's showpiece oversight surface) does not carry its weight: the panel text is illegible at print size while the caption describes details the reader cannot see ('each entry shows the citing sentence to check, the recorded evidence, the access link...'). Worse, the screenshot itself shows a rendering defect — the preview title reads 'F(AI) 2 R: ... Who Checked?\\ Verifiable...' with a literal LaTeX line-break — and a 'commit 30d990c +dirty' badge, i.e., the provenance paper's own oversight screenshot was taken from an uncommitted working tree. A zoomed reader also finds unexplained categories ('34 human-verified, 20 internal, 0 not yet ready (65 total)') that do not reconcile on the page with Table II's 67 sources.

Fig. 2 largely duplicates Table I: both list the same seven rungs, and the figure's margin notes ('human-only', 'access gate for 5-6', 'highest AI-grantable') restate the table's 'who may grant' column. In a page-limited paper one of the two should go.

The Fig. 6 dashboard tiles disagree with Table II by more than 2x (cost USD 736.95 vs ~1577; output tokens 1.83M vs 2.46M). The caption's one-clause explanation (per-activity sums vs session-record aggregates) does not tell the reader why over half the cost has no per-activity record, or which number is authoritative — a confusing gap in a paper about exact accounting.

Verbatim self-repetition between Sections I and III: 'publish-or-perish pays for counted output, and hypercompetition selects for whatever maximizes the count' appears in both, with the same citation; the intro's third paragraph pre-empts much of Section III, which makes the dilution section feel padded and delays the technical contribution to Section IV (page 3).

Apposition-heavy sentences repeatedly force re-reading. Examples: 'Provider-side provenance, signed inference records carrying model, timestamps, usage, roles, and prompt/response hashes, would eliminate that class of misreporting...' (comma-delimited appositive inside a comma list, Sec. VII); 'the operator granted the first human-confirmed against a vendored statute text the gate handed over, confirmed the five self-cited sources they authored, the class where the human's judgement is uniquely authoritative, and then walked the queue...' (Sec. VI). Em-dashes or parentheses would fix most of these.

Terminology layering burdens the first-time reader: F(AI)²R names the title, the 'original experiment' (a different repository), and the stance; aiprov names the actual vocabulary; 'the skill' / 'ai-provenance' names the packaging. The abstract's 'Building on the original F(AI)²R experiment' is opaque to anyone who does not already know a prior experiment exists, and 'publishes the current build of this very paper' is confusing before the self-application is explained. 'Harness' (Sec. VI/VII) and 'CFRP' are never defined; 'AAS' is used as an acronym without ever being introduced as one.

Concrete copy/layout defects verified in the PDF: 'inside a 89-hour wall-clock span' should be 'an 89-hour' (p. 7); 'artifact digests' (Sec. V) vs 'artefact' everywhere else; Table III's 'Count' column contains unit-bearing entries ('2 036 w', '12.1 h'); Fig. 8's caption is telegraphic ('metrics single source; classification as in the text'); no IEEE Index Terms; PDF metadata Title/Author fields are empty; a sentence begins with lowercase 'shepard' (Sec. VII).
questions: What is the criterion for promoting an assertion to a first-class aiprov:Claim? Eight claims for a 12-page paper implies heavy curation — who chose them, and is that choice itself logged?

Fig. 6's per-activity cost/token tiles cover less than half of the session-record totals in Table II. What fraction of activities lack per-activity telemetry, and can the caption quantify the coverage gap so the reader knows which number is authoritative?

Is 'the demonstration shows every rung in use' meant historically (rungs transited during promotions) rather than in the final distribution? Fig. 6 shows needs-research and reference-resolved at zero.

Can Fig. 5 be replaced by a legible crop (e.g., one queue entry at readable size), and will the preview-page title rendering ('F(AI) 2 R', literal '\\') and the '+dirty' commit badge be fixed before camera-ready?

If the Discussion had to shrink to roughly a page, which of its ~13 topics do you consider load-bearing, and could copyright, 'nostalgia for the paper', and the force-multiplier reading move to a supplementary note or the repository?

The paper says the queue shows '65 total' sources while Table II reports 67 on the ladder, and Fig. 5 mentions '20 internal' sources — can these categories be reconciled somewhere a reader will find them?
